The engine is a three-tier, header-first C++20/CUDA codebase with a strict separation between interface (`include/strata/`, 118 headers, ~12.3k lines) and implementation (`src/`, 183 files, ~88.2k lines of `.cpp`/`.cu`).

It is organised as eleven modules that mirror eleven CMake libraries, and the dependency graph is acyclic and layered: `artifact → plan → core → kernels → engine → prefill → program`, with `spec` and `ngram` as side branches consumed only by the driver.

CUDA is the native dialect; AMD is reached by a header shim (`include/strata/hip_compat/`, `include/strata/platform/hip_compat/`) that redefines `cuda_runtime.h`/`cublas_v2.h` onto HIP so "the engine's sources stay one tree" (`include/strata/platform/hip_compat/strata_hip.h:2-6`).
Intel Arc is a separate project (`sycl/`, 202 files) that reuses the same `src/` and is mutually exclusive at configure time (`CMakeLists.txt:14-20`).

`third_party` is a narrow, pinned dependency: only ggml is consumed, and only three files are vendored in-tree; the build normally FetchContent-pulls llama.cpp at commit `3cf03257f219afbe7334045ff7c6a06ac68c627d` (2026-09-20).
`core ↔ kernels` is the dominant coupling (112 + 7 edges).
`program` is the only consumer of `spec` and of `prefill` — spec/prefill are not part of the core.
`artifact` and `plan` are leaf modules with no GPU dependency, which is deliberate: `strata_artifact` and `strata_plan` are `INTERFACE` libraries with no CUDA link (`CMakeLists.txt:227, 258`).

This is a cross-cutting layer, not a directory: Quant-format capability is likewise compile-gated: `STRATA_MMQ_KQUANTS` (Q4_K/Q5_K/Q5_1/Q6_K), `STRATA_Q6K_EXPERTS`, `STRATA_ORCA_Q4KS_MMQ`, `STRATA_NATIVE_EXPERTS`.
It is not referenced by the build — no `third_party/llama.cpp` path appears in `CMakeLists.txt`, `setup.py`, or `setup.sh`.

Actual ggml surface used is tiny and specific: 16 source/header files include `ggml.h`, `ggml-cpu.h`, or `ggml-common.h`, concentrated in `src/kernels/cpu/{iq_avx2,iq_avx512,kq_avx2,native_expert}.cpp`, `src/kernels/cuda/iq_kernels.cu`, `src/prefill/moe_fused_iq.cu`, and `src/core/mtp.cpp`.
Link is only `ggml-cpu` + `ggml-base` (`CMakeLists.txt:1158`).

asks: Make a report about how /home/ai-user0/HyperCore-WebUI derives the token counts per second for decode, thinking, prefill, bus (from ssd, from ram, from cpu) and the rate for any token traffic not listed here.
what are the actual core code phases of the system?
Which of these have transfer rates that can be monitored to to identify the impact of the engines flags and associated values?

How can this be transferred into /home/ai-user0/opyuna_tune to ensure when the best possible performance -> system resource balance is reached? Done — the transfer telemetry is now wired into the tuner. Here's how it works and what changed.
outcomes: Short answer: there are exactly two clocks in the system — the engine's C++ `steady_clock` and the server's Python `time.time()` — and every "tok/s" number is a division of one of those.

Decode and prefill are real rates; thinking has no rate of its own; and the SSD/RAM/CPU "bus" figures are per-token counts and per-token milliseconds, not rates — anything that reads like a bus rate is that count multiplied by the decode rate.

`serve/server.py:94` is explicit about why the live number is a window rather than a mean: a mean reads `1/elapsed` at the first token (the Monitor showed five-digit numbers) and undershoots for the first second.
`serve/test_server.py:844` (`LiveRate`) is the test that pins that behaviour.

Note the multi-GPU/pipelined path counts tokens per engine idle period (`multi_n`), so its `tok_s` is an aggregate across concurrent requests, while each request's own `DONE` still carries its `produced` and `decode_ms`.
There is no thinking rate. `in_think` is a state flag (`generate.cpp:1716`, `:2003`); reasoning tokens are counted in the same `produced`/`generated` counter as answer tokens.

The thinking budget is enforced in tokens (`produced >= req_think_budget` → force `</think>`), and the loop guard uses different windows while thinking (`STRATA_GLM_LOOP_THINK` 256 vs `_ANSWER` 1024).
The only thinking-specific output is the phase label — `_note()` sets `s["phase"] = "thinking"` for `ev.kind == "reasoning"` — so the dashboard shows "thinking" with the decode tok/s attached.

Per MoE route of `K` experts, `glm_fast_path.cu:3700–3776` partitions every routed expert into exactly one bucket: So the reported quantities are counts per token (`ram_fetch`, `disk`, `promo`, `cpu_experts` — the dashboard's unit is literally `/tok`, `app.js:263-277`) and milliseconds per token (`disk_ms/tok`, `cpu_ms/tok`).
`tools/glm_cache_sim.py` and `tools/glm_tier_replay.py` simulate the same accounting (`reads/tok`, `MB/tok`, `vram%`, `ram%`, `off-card ms/tok`).

The actual bus bandwidth is measured separately (`stream_bandwidth()`, and `load_main.cpp:84` — "the bus is the ceiling, so measure it at the granularity the engine actually uses"), because a 1.38 MB copy does not reach the bus's rated throughput.
Everything else is the complement of the listed counters, and its rate is always `decode_rate × (per-token count)`:
`tok_s` (live) and `decode_tok_s` (per request) can disagree: one is a 2 s window, the other a whole-request mean.
The engine's `STAT` lines are emitted every 8 tokens; the server keeps only the last 120 in `stat_history` for sparklines.
The CPU lane is not a byte stream: `pcie_share` decides how many of those experts are copied over PCIe versus computed on the CPU, so `cpu_experts/tok` and `ram_fetch/tok` trade against each other.

outcomes: Both parts are in `/home/ai-user0/HyperCore-WebUI/optuna_tune`, tested, and the state file is updated (loop 12).

`off-card` is the share of the decode's routed experts the GPU did not get from its own VRAM: DONE position 15 (`offloaded`, #588) against the cache lookups, exactly the number the engine prints beside its hit rate (`src/program/generate.cpp:10435-10439`).
`optuna_tune/stub_engine.py`: emits the decode counters (8 experts per generated token, the `--pcie-frac` share off-card) so the field table is testable.

`optuna_tune/winner_bench.py` (new), one command in the shape of `/home/ai-user0/Strata/setup.sh --setup` / `./bench.sh`: reads the deliverable `max_run_<model>.json`, checks the card with nvidia-smi, boots the engine with that config's own args (`--serve`/`--max-new` added back), and reports per-boot lines plus medians with the off-card share, then the delta against what the sweep recorded.
The GPU is still busy, so the winner confirmation run (`--repeat 3` against the q2_0 winner) is queued in the state file for when the card frees.
The engine's `#588` counter is the problem, not the parser.
10240 0`: `offloaded` is 0 at every `--pcie-frac` from 0.01 to 0.26, while `hits`/`lookups` are populated.
The populated counters are the decode cache misses: `lookups - hits` are the routed experts the VRAM cache did not hold (admitted from the pack over PCIe, or refused and computed by the CPU pool).
That is the same number the engine prints beside its hit rate (`generate.cpp:10435-10439`).

`prompt_transfer.py` now takes the union: `off_card_pct = 100 (offloaded + (lookups - hits)) / (lookups + offloaded)`, records which counter it came from (`engine-offload`, `cache-miss`, `both`, `on-card`), and stores `cache_hits` as a transfer column.
That is worth knowing before the next sweep: the `pcie` dimension is not moving the decode's off-card traffic on this build.
`stub_engine.py --token-graph` reproduces the hit path (`offloaded 0`, `hits < lookups`) so the fallback is exercised, not assumed.
`bash -n max_tune.sh` and `py_compile` on all four changed files: clean.
`ruff` on the changed files reports only pre-existing findings.
`winner_bench.py` now records `generated_median` per rung, prints `decoded N tok`, and flags a rung whose median decode is under half of `--max-new` as not comparable.

The equivalent is `STRATA_ROUTE_TAIL_SKIP`, and it is present in `/home/ai-user0/Strata` only as tooling and docs:
Default-on exclusion set: HyperCore also excludes `remote_count > 0`; Strata excludes only `peer_device` and `--batch`.
`src/program/generate.cpp:10459-10461`: It is printed at the end of each request's stats block, next to the cache-hit-rate and expert-tier lines.
`HYPERCORE_ROUTE_TAIL_SKIP=7` (the CUDA serve default, set at `generate.cpp:6904`) makes the CPU expert dispatch drop whole tails of experts that are not in any tier.
For each token, count `cnt` = how many of its 10 routed experts are not in the VRAM tier (`host_res[...] < 0`), not on a peer GPU, and not held by a helper/remote GPU.
In the compute loop (`:2794-2797`) the row is `memset(row, 0, H4)` instead of being computed.
Note the double increment: HyperCore adds the distinct count at `:2658` and then again per entry at `:2796`, so the parenthetical is `distinct + routed slots`, not the routed-slot count alone.
Strata 1.42 increments `tail_skipped` only in the entry loop (`/home/ai-user0/Strata_1.42/src/core/expert_source.cpp:3768`), so there the parenthetical is the true entry count.
`--batch` slots, a peer GPU, or a remote/helper GPU: the default is not set (`generate.cpp:6906-6908`), and the dispatch guard excludes them.
A window of one token: `n_tok > 1` is required (`expert_source.cpp:2612`).

The doc comment at `include/hypercore/core/expert_source.hpp:431` describes the Strata rule ("a missed expert that every token of the window routes that low"), but HyperCore's implementation is per-token (`cnt >= 7`), while Strata 1.42 is per-expert via `minr[q] >= tail_rank` (`/home/ai-user0/Strata_1.42/src/core/expert_source.cpp:3592-3612`).

Diff against the backup — exactly the four changes, nothing else: Plus the profile alignment: `strata-q2_0.shared-settings.json` copied to `ni_strata-q2_0.shared-settings.json`, so the Chat-tab defaults (temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, reasoning_effort high) now belong to the profile that's actually running.

`svc.config_path` and the engine `args` are read at startup, and `ensure_loaded()` reuses that args list — so a `/v1/unload` + `/v1/load` cycle will not pick up `--vram-reserve-mib`.
`effort_position: "end"` needs engine ≥ 0.1.39.

You're on 0.1.40, so it will apply; on startup it prints `effort_position end: a request's non-default reasoning effort goes right before the answer, so changing it keeps the cached conversation` and adds `--tail-role-token` to the args.

It is organised as eleven modules that mirror eleven CMake libraries, and the dependency graph is acyclic and layered: `artifact → plan → core → kernels → engine → prefill → program`, with `spec` and `ngram` as side branches consumed only by the driver.

CUDA is the native dialect; AMD is reached by a header shim (`include/strata/hip_compat/`, `include/strata/platform/hip_compat/`) that redefines `cuda_runtime.h`/`cublas_v2.h` onto HIP so "the engine's sources stay one tree" (`include/strata/platform/hip_compat/strata_hip.h:2-6`).
Intel Arc is a separate project (`sycl/`, 202 files) that reuses the same `src/` and is mutually exclusive at configure time (`CMakeLists.txt:14-20`).

`artifact` and `plan` are leaf modules with no GPU dependency, which is deliberate: `strata_artifact` and `strata_plan` are `INTERFACE` libraries with no CUDA link (`CMakeLists.txt:227, 258`).

outcomes: The engine is a three-tier, header-first C++20/CUDA codebase with a strict separation between interface (`include/strata/`, 118 headers, ~12.3k lines) and implementation (`src/`, 183 files, ~88.2k lines of `.cpp`/`.cu`).

It is organised as eleven modules that mirror eleven CMake libraries, and the dependency graph is acyclic and layered: `artifact → plan → core → kernels → engine → prefill → program`, with `spec` and `ngram` as side branches consumed only by the driver.

One source tree, three GPU backends. CUDA is the native dialect; AMD is reached by a header shim (`include/strata/hip_compat/`, `include/strata/platform/hip_compat/`) that redefines `cuda_runtime.h`/`cublas_v2.h` onto HIP so "the engine's sources stay one tree" (`include/strata/platform/hip_compat/strata_hip.h:2-6`).
Intel Arc is a separate project (`sycl/`, 202 files) that reuses the same `src/` and is mutually exclusive at configure time (`CMakeLists.txt:14-20`).

`third_party` is a narrow, pinned dependency: only ggml is consumed, and only three files are vendored in-tree; the build normally FetchContent-pulls llama.cpp at commit `3cf03257f219afbe7334045ff7c6a06ac68c627d` (2026-09-20).
`core ↔ kernels` is the dominant coupling (112 + 7 edges).
`program` is the only consumer of `spec` and of `prefill` — spec/prefill are not part of the core.
`artifact` and `plan` are leaf modules with no GPU dependency, which is deliberate: `strata_artifact` and `strata_plan` are `INTERFACE` libraries with no CUDA link (`CMakeLists.txt:227, 258`).

This is a cross-cutting layer, not a directory: Quant-format capability is likewise compile-gated: `STRATA_MMQ_KQUANTS` (Q4_K/Q5_K/Q5_1/Q6_K), `STRATA_Q6K_EXPERTS`, `STRATA_ORCA_Q4KS_MMQ`, `STRATA_NATIVE_EXPERTS`.
It is not referenced by the build — no `third_party/llama.cpp` path appears in `CMakeLists.txt`, `setup.py`, or `setup.sh`.

Actual ggml surface used is tiny and specific: 16 source/header files include `ggml.h`, `ggml-cpu.h`, or `ggml-common.h`, concentrated in `src/kernels/cpu/{iq_avx2,iq_avx512,kq_avx2,native_expert}.cpp`, `src/kernels/cuda/iq_kernels.cu`, `src/prefill/moe_fused_iq.cu`, and `src/core/mtp.cpp`.
Link is only `ggml-cpu` + `ggml-base` (`CMakeLists.txt:1158`).
Structural implication: llama.cpp is vendored as a reference/upstream mirror, not as a linked dependency.

Parity/bench/test files are colocated with the kernels they check (`src/kernels/_parity.cpp`), plus a separate `tests/` tree: `tests/core` 12 files, `tests/hip` 16, `tests/cuda` 3, `tests/prefill` 1, `tests/platform` 1, `tests/data/native_experts` 6 fixtures.
The pattern is systematic: every GPU kernel in `src/kernels/cuda/` has a CPU or reference counterpart driven from `src/kernels/` — e.g.

outcomes: A `StrataEngine` class and a JSON→`Options` mapper are both implementations of a boundary; if the boundary is undefined, you end up with a class that happens to be CUDA-shaped and a config mapper that can't be tested against anything.

`strata_session_t` is the wrong unit. The engine already owns conversation state: a request continues "from the live session or the longest conversation checkpoint its prompt starts with" (generate.cpp:5036).
Requests are the unit; conversation reuse is inside the box, observable through `summary.prompt_reused`.
Per-request sampling is on the hot path and needs validation (`top_k` must be 1..64).
`CMakeLists.txt` has no library target at all today — only `add_executable` and `INTERFACE` libs — so the `.so` needs a target too.

Do internal `std::exit()` paths become error codes, or does the box stay crash-on-error and the embedder accepts a lost process? This determines whether the `.so` is embeddable at all, and it's the largest single piece of work in the refactor.

Is the SYCL/HIP side expected to implement this contract, or is the `.so` CUDA-only for v1? If the 25-header `sycl/` tree is meant to implement it, the contract needs a capability-negotiation step now — otherwise you ship a C API that is a CUDA wrapper with a neutral name, which is the failure mode your third decision was specifically trying to avoid.
If the host application submits a request when all concurrent slots configured via --batch are full, the engine will refuse the payload.
For example, if a consumer sends top_k = 128, it returns STRATA_STATUS_INVALID_ARG immediately rather than bubbling down to src/kernels/sampler.cu and causing an abrupt std::exit().
`<cstdlib>`, `<cstring>`, `<new>` are missing.
`run(cfg, say, start_engine)` takes `start_engine` as an injected parameter, and `tools/test_calibrate.py` already injects a stand-in.
Add those two fields to the request config — that's exactly what `struct_size` is for.
Either is fine; both are additive, and neither is expressible with the current `strata_output_chunk_t`.

Files are in `bench/results/2026-10-09-blackbox-api/`: `strata_bridge_review.cpp` (as written), `strata_bridge_fixed.cpp` (compiles, 5 exported entry points), `abi_test.c` and `busy_test.c` (both pass).
Script is at `tools/daytona_bridge_test.py`; it's `ruff`-clean.

The engine is a three-tier, header-first C++20/CUDA codebase with a strict separation between interface (`include/strata/`, 118 headers, ~12.3k lines) and implementation (`src/`, 183 files, ~88.2k lines of `.cpp`/`.cu`).

It is organised as eleven modules that mirror eleven CMake libraries, and the dependency graph is acyclic and layered: `artifact → plan → core → kernels → engine → prefill → program`, with `spec` and `ngram` as side branches consumed only by the driver.

One source tree, three GPU backends. CUDA is the native dialect; AMD is reached by a header shim (`include/strata/hip_compat/`, `include/strata/platform/hip_compat/`) that redefines `cuda_runtime.h`/`cublas_v2.h` onto HIP so "the engine's sources stay one tree" (`include/strata/platform/hip_compat/strata_hip.h:2-6`).
Intel Arc is a separate project (`sycl/`, 202 files) that reuses the same `src/` and is mutually exclusive at configure time (`CMakeLists.txt:14-20`).

`third_party` is a narrow, pinned dependency: only ggml is consumed, and only three files are vendored in-tree; the build normally FetchContent-pulls llama.cpp at commit `3cf03257f219afbe7334045ff7c6a06ac68c627d` (2026-09-20).
`core ↔ kernels` is the dominant coupling (112 + 7 edges).
`program` is the only consumer of `spec` and of `prefill` — spec/prefill are not part of the core.
`artifact` and `plan` are leaf modules with no GPU dependency, which is deliberate: `strata_artifact` and `strata_plan` are `INTERFACE` libraries with no CUDA link (`CMakeLists.txt:227, 258`).

This is a cross-cutting layer, not a directory: Quant-format capability is likewise compile-gated: `STRATA_MMQ_KQUANTS` (Q4_K/Q5_K/Q5_1/Q6_K), `STRATA_Q6K_EXPERTS`, `STRATA_ORCA_Q4KS_MMQ`, `STRATA_NATIVE_EXPERTS`.
It is not referenced by the build — no `third_party/llama.cpp` path appears in `CMakeLists.txt`, `setup.py`, or `setup.sh`.

Actual ggml surface used is tiny and specific: 16 source/header files include `ggml.h`, `ggml-cpu.h`, or `ggml-common.h`, concentrated in `src/kernels/cpu/{iq_avx2,iq_avx512,kq_avx2,native_expert}.cpp`, `src/kernels/cuda/iq_kernels.cu`, `src/prefill/moe_fused_iq.cu`, and `src/core/mtp.cpp`.

Structural implication: llama.cpp is vendored as a reference/upstream mirror, not as a linked dependency.
